matching.reasoningTemplate: Encephalopathy with stigmata of chronic liver disease suggests hepatic encephalopathy — seek a precipitant.

harrison.pages: Harrison 22e p.2716-2717 (HE in cirrhosis), p.230-231 (pathophysiology of metabolic/hepatic encephalopathy), p.2629-2630 (signs of hepatic failure)
clinicalPearls: Hepatic encephalopathy is far more common in chronic liver disease than in acute liver injury; in severe acute liver injury its presence is itself a defining criterion for acute liver failure (Harrison 22e p.2716).

Asterixis (the 'liver flap') is typically present and is elicited by having the patient extend the arms and dorsiflex the wrists, looking for a sudden forward jerk of the wrist; it requires a cooperative patient (Harrison 22e p.2716).

Earliest manifestations are subtle and nonspecific: altered sleep pattern, personality change, irritability, and mental dullness, progressing to confusion, disorientation, stupor and coma (Harrison 22e p.2629).
Patients may be agitated, violent and hard to manage, or alternatively very sleepy and difficult to rouse (Harrison 22e p.2716).
In acute liver failure, presentation may include excitability or mania rather than depressed consciousness (Harrison 22e p.2629).
Fetor hepaticus, a sweetish ammoniacal breath odor, can accompany liver failure, especially with portosystemic shunting of blood (Harrison 22e p.2629).
After a first episode, patients and caregivers often learn to recognize recurrences early and can self-medicate to prevent worsening (Harrison 22e p.2717).
Gut-derived neurotoxins that bypass the liver because of vascular shunting and reduced hepatic mass reach the brain and produce the syndrome (Harrison 22e p.2716).
harrison.pathophysiology: Hepatic encephalopathy is an alteration of mental status and cognition resulting from liver failure, in which gut-derived neurotoxins are not cleared because of portosystemic vascular shunting and decreased functional hepatic mass and thus reach the brain. Ammonia is the principal candidate toxin: high ammonia concentrations are thought to drive increased synthesis of glutamine within astrocytes, causing osmotic astrocyte swelling, mitochondrial energy failure, and generation of reactive nitrogen and oxygen species, together with increased levels of the inhibitory neurotransmitter GABA and synthesis of putative 'false' neurotransmitters. No single one of these mechanisms fully explains the confusion and stupor, and which is mainly responsible for hepatic coma is not known. Other contributing compounds include certain false neurotransmitters and mercaptans. Chronic HE is characteristically accompanied by diffuse astrocytosis. In acute liver failure (but not chronic liver disease) cerebral edema with gray-matter swelling can occur and carries a risk of cerebral herniation (Harrison 22e p.230-231, p.2716).
additionalDifferentials: Other causes of altered mental status must always be considered, since the diagnosis is clinical (Harrison 22e p.2716)
Electrolyte imbalance as a primary cause of confusion (Harrison 22e p.2629)
nonInfectiousMimics: Metabolic encephalopathy from other causes (hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, hyperosmolar states, hypercapnia, hypercalcemia, renal failure) — asterixis and multifocal myoclonus are nonspecific and indicate a metabolic or toxic process generally, not HE specifically (Harrison 22e p.230, p.225)
Drug intoxication, which likewise can produce asterixis in a drowsy, confused patient (Harrison 22e p.231)
Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome and alcohol withdrawal in patients with alcohol-associated liver disease (Harrison 22e p.2674)
additionalInvestigations: Careful mental status examination is the central assessment (Harrison 22e p.2629)
Trail-making (connect-the-dots / number-connection) test: normal 15-30 s, markedly prolonged in early HE (Harrison 22e p.2629)
Bedside cognitive tasks such as drawing abstract objects or comparing the patient's signature with prior examples (Harrison 22e p.2629)
Diagnostic paracentesis of ascites to exclude infection as a precipitant (Harrison 22e p.2716)
EEG and visual evoked potentials can detect mild forms but are rarely clinically useful (Harrison 22e p.2629)
redFlags: Encephalopathy appearing during acute hepatitis is the major criterion for acute liver failure and indicates a poor prognosis (Harrison 22e p.2629)
In acute liver failure, severe encephalopathy with cerebral edema can progress to cerebral herniation (Harrison 22e p.2716)
Other presenting features of poor prognosis in acute hepatitis: ascites, peripheral edema, prolonged PT, hypoalbuminemia, hypoglycemia, very high bilirubin (Harrison 22e p.2672)
HE may herald acute-on-chronic liver failure (brain is one of the failing organ systems), which carries 28-day mortality of 20-70% rising with the number of organ failures (Harrison 22e p.2717)
harrison.prognosis: Development of hepatic encephalopathy in chronic liver disease is a poor prognostic sign, although the complication can be managed in the vast majority of patients. Hepatic encephalopathy grade is one of the five Child-Pugh variables (with bilirubin, albumin, prothrombin time, and ascites severity) used to stratify cirrhosis into classes A-C of predicted survival. In acute hepatitis, the appearance of encephalopathy defines acute liver failure and indicates poor prognosis (Harrison 22e p.2717, p.2629).
pitfalls: Ammonia levels are typically elevated but correlate poorly with severity of liver disease; most hepatologists do not rely on ammonia to make the diagnosis or to follow clinical progress (Harrison 22e p.2716).

Always identify and treat a precipitant — in cirrhosis, encephalopathy is usually triggered by volume depletion/dehydration, GI bleeding, infection, constipation, hyponatremia, overdiuresis, uremia, electrolyte imbalance, or sedatives/narcotic analgesics; correcting hydration and electrolytes alone is sometimes sufficient (Harrison 22e p.2629, p.2716).
Asterixis is nonspecific — it also occurs in other metabolic and toxic encephalopathies, so it does not by itself establish HE (Harrison 22e p.230-231).
The diagnosis is clinical and requires an experienced clinician to integrate the various features; there is no single confirmatory test (Harrison 22e p.2716).
harrison.severityClassification: Severity is graded clinically along a continuum from the earliest covert/subtle changes (altered sleep, personality change, irritability, mental dullness — detectable mainly by mental-status testing such as the trail-making test) through confusion and disorientation to stupor and coma. Encephalopathy grade is incorporated as one component of the Child-Pugh classification of cirrhosis severity. (Note: Harrison 22e describes this graded clinical spectrum and 'grade' in the Child-Pugh score but the supplied text does not lay out the explicit numbered West Haven criteria; Harrison 22e p.2629, p.2716, p.2715/HCC staging.)

valueTables.title: Treatment of hepatic encephalopathy

cells.text: Infection, bleeding, hypokalaemia, dehydration, diuretics, sedatives
Titrate to 2 or 3 soft stools daily; by tube if comatose
Add to lactulose or if not tolerated
Also look for a large spontaneous shunt to embolise
